summary.text: 地 is a phonosemantic character: 土 marks the earth-related meaning, while 也 supplies a historical sound cue. Its common noun senses include earth, ground, land and region. [ref013][ref015]

formation.text: The received analysis is phonosemantic: 土 contributes the meaning category, and 也 contributes sound. Shuowen records this analysis in the Eastern Han; it is an early explicit account, not proof of the graph’s earliest design. [ref013][ref016]

components.text: 土 is the left component in the received analysis. It contributes the earth-related meaning category; its role here is semantic, not a claim that the whole character depicts a scene. [ref013]
也 is the right component in the received analysis and supplies a sound cue. Its own original referent is unsettled, so it is not treated here as a depicted object in 地. [ref013][ref017]

sound_limitation.text: The cited reconstructions support a historical sound relationship within the Zhengzhang system, but are reconstructions rather than recordings and do not by themselves prove the component’s original design rationale. [ref016][ref018]

sound.text: Zhengzhang Old Chinese 地 *l'els and 也 *laːlʔ are compatible with an approximate historical sound relationship; modern Mandarin dì and yě differ. [ref016]

history.text: The curated late Western Zhou bronze redraw shows a form whose right element is identified as 它 in a catalog account; the seal-script redraw shows the received 土-plus-也 analysis. The proposed 它-to-也 regularization is a reported interpretation, not a change established by the drawings alone, and neither image proves the earliest design. [ref014][ref026][ref013][ref027]

地 is also associated with the graph 墬 in lexicographic discussion. One proposal treats 墬 as an earlier graph for the earth sense, but the evidence does not settle whether it is an ancestor, a parallel form or a replaced graph. [ref022][ref023]

uncertainties.text: The evidence supports the received 土-plus-也 account and records competing interpretations of earlier forms. No inspected inscription image or primary paleographic study here establishes the earliest graphic design or the proposed 它-to-也 history. [ref013][ref014]

senses.text: The earliest inspectable evidence in this dossier is the Han-period Shuowen entry, which describes 地 as the heavy, turbid yin counterpart to heaven and as where things are arrayed. This is an attested lexicographic account, not proof that this was the word’s hypothetical original meaning. [ref003][ref013]

Cited texts document uses for ground, cultivated land, territory and place or region, among other noun senses. Their citation does not establish the first occurrence of each sense or a complete sequence of semantic change. [ref015][ref025]

senses.gloss: grammatical particle after an adjective, commonly read de
senses.period: Song citation; exact first use unresolved
senses.text: A Song text is cited for adjective-following 地. The attestation establishes this use in the cited textual tradition, but not how it arose from the noun or another form. [ref015][ref019]

senses.period: Yuan citation; exact first use unresolved
senses.text: A Yuan text is cited for a postverbal use glossed as ‘stand there/remain’; the evidence does not establish its precise relation to other uses of 地. [ref019]

developments.text: Earth/ground and land or territory belong to the documented noun uses, but the dossier does not establish the stages or dates linking them. [ref015][ref025]

One proposal derives the manner particle through an ‘adjective place’ to ‘in an adjective manner’ path. Other analyses connect it to 的 or demonstrative/interrogative forms; none establishes a single derivation or complete sequence. [ref020][ref021]

limitations.text: Classical work citations do not independently date the surviving wording, and the first attestations and semantic bridges among noun senses remain unresolved. [ref015][ref019][ref025]
The particle’s relation to the noun 地, 的, or demonstrative/interrogative forms remains disputed; the evidence does not establish one historical pathway. [ref020][ref021]

overview.text: 地 means earth or ground and is also used for land and place. 土 marks the meaning category; 也 supplies a historical sound cue, though its modern Mandarin reading differs. [ref013][ref016]

components.text: 土 points to the earth-related meaning of the character. [ref013]
也 supplies the historical sound cue; its own original referent is not settled. [ref016][ref017]

takeaway.text: The adjective-following particle use is attested, but its connection to the earth/ground noun remains disputed. [ref019][ref021]

relationships.text: In the received analysis of 地, 土 contributes the earth-related meaning category. [ref013]
The received analysis assigns 也 a sound role; historical reconstructions support an approximate relationship, while not proving the graph’s original design. [ref013][ref016]
